general_information.Description: This course introduces blockchain technology and its applications in cryptocurrencies and decentralized finance (DeFi). It covers cryptographic primitives (hash functions, digital signatures), blockchain data structures (blocks, Merkle trees), network architecture (nodes, mempool), consensus mechanisms and security (PoW/PoS, forks, double spending, 51% attack), and the evolution from Bitcoin to smart-contract platforms. The DeFi part focuses on financial primitives and protocols such as stablecoins, decentralized exchanges and automated market makers (AMMs), liquidity pools, tokenization and NFTs, governance via DAOs, and key issues in risk management, security, and regulation. Students will practice using wallets, block explorers, and smart-contract sandboxes; analyze real-world DeFi cases and on-chain data; and propose a DeFi/FinTech solution with clear assumptions, risks, and compliance considerations.
general_information.StudentTasks: Students must attend at least 80% of contact sessions to be eligible for the final assessment. - Complete required readings and pre-class preparation; actively participate in discussions, case analyses, and in-class exercises. Complete and submit all quizzes/assignments/labs/projects on time; contribute fairly and professionally in group work. Follow academic integrity rules (no plagiarism, proper citation, no unauthorized collaboration); use AI tools responsibly and transparently when allowed by the instructor. - Use laptops/tablets in class strictly for learning activities. For hands-on blockchain labs: use testnets/sandbox accounts unless explicitly instructed; do NOT share private keys/seed phrases; follow security best practices.
general_information.Note: Notes: - Blockchain & DeFi evolve rapidly; readings, examples, and tool versions may be updated during the semester. - The course is for educational purposes only and is NOT investment advice. - Students are not required to use real funds; labs can be completed fully on test networks.

It covers cryptographic primitives (hash functions, digital signatures), blockchain data structures (blocks, Merkle trees), network architecture (nodes, mempool), consensus mechanisms and security (PoW/PoS, forks, double spending, 51% attack), and the evolution from Bitcoin to smart-contract platforms. The DeFi part focuses on financial primitives and protocols such as stablecoins, decentralized exchanges and automated market makers (AMMs), liquidity pools, tokenization and NFTs, governance via DAOs, and key issues in risk management, security, and regulation. Students will practice using wallets, block explorers, and smart-contract sandboxes; analyze real-world DeFi cases and on-chain data; and propose a DeFi/FinTech solution with clear assumptions, risks, and compliance considerations.

learning_outcomes.CLO Details: Explain blockchain fundamentals and describe how consensus mechanisms of PoW, PoS prevent double spending and maintain transaction integrity.
Describe the operating principles of Ethereum, smart contracts, gas fee economics, oracles and identify basic scaling approaches (Layer 1 sharding vs. Layer 2 rollups & payment channels).
Differentiate between stablecoin models and CBDCs, explaining their peg mechanisms and operational and liquidity risks.
Explain core DeFi market mechanisms, including Automated Market Makers, liquidity pools (impermanent loss), DAO governance models, and real-world asset tokenization.
Practice essential Web3 user operations, including setting up and securing non-custodial wallets, key management, executing testnet transactions, and participating in basic DAO voting.
Demonstrate basic DeFi user interactions on testnets and use public blockchain explorers/analytics dashboards to track transactions and protocol metrics.

assessments.Knowledge and Skill: In-depth case analysis of a prominent real-world DeFi protocol (e.g., MakerDAO, Uniswap, Compound, Aave) or tokenization model; extracting on-chain metrics via DefiLlama/Etherscan, explaining protocol workflow, and identifying basic operational and liquidity risks.
assessments.Grading Guide: Group work (4–5 students). Select an approved protocol, explore its user interface, summarize metrics and risks, submit slides, and present live in class

assessments.Question Type: Practical execution on Testnet + Submit transaction hashes / screenshots
assessments.Knowledge and Skill: Hands-on execution of essential Web3 and DeFi user operations on zero-cost public testnets: Setting up MetaMask wallet & safely storing the 12-word seed phrase, Requesting free testnet tokens from faucets & executing a peer-to-peer transfer, Looking up transactions, addresses, and gas fees on Etherscan block explorer, Executing a simple token swap on a testnet DEX (Uniswap) & adjusting slippage
assessments.Grading Guide: Students complete 4 guided practical exercises in class with step-by-step instructions.

assessments.Knowledge and Skill: Basic concepts of blockchain, hashing, blocks, P2P networks, PoW/PoS consensus, Bitcoin transactions, Ethereum, smart contracts, gas fees, and scaling ideas
assessments.Grading Guide: Conducted in-class via CMS/LMS system during Session.

assessments.Knowledge and Skill: Basic stablecoin types (fiat-backed, DAI), CBDCs, DApps & DAOs, simple lending concepts, AMM swap principles (x⋅y=k), liquidity pools, and real-world asset tokenization
assessments.Grading Guide: Conducted in-class via CMS/LMS system during Session.

assessments.Knowledge and Skill: Comprehensive assessment of foundational concepts and core mechanisms across Chapters 1 to 9 (Blockchain architecture, PoW/PoS consensus, Smart contracts, Gas fees, Scalability L1/L2, Stablecoins, CBDCs, DAOs, Lending pools, AMM constant product formula, Liquidity pools, and RWAs).
assessments.Grading Guide: University centralized computer-based exam organized by the Exam Board

constructive_questions.Name: CQ1
constructive_questions.Details: Why isn’t blockchain “just an Excel database”? Identify which properties are essential for DeFi, and justify with one concrete DeFi use case.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ2
constructive_questions.Details: In a trustless setting (no bank), how can a digital payment system prevent double spending?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ1
constructive_questions.Details: A single transaction in a block is modified. Why does this matter for scalability and light verification?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ1
constructive_questions.Details: Two miners produce two valid blocks at the same height. Explain how a P2P network resolves this fork. What does “finality” mean for DeFi trades and liquidations?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ1
constructive_questions.Details: Miners/validators spend resources to secure the network. Using incentives, explain why honest behavior can be rational. Under what conditions could attacks become more feasible?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ2
constructive_questions.Details: During congestion, how are transactions selected from the mempool (fees, size, waiting time, validity)?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ3
constructive_questions.Details: What are the impacts on DeFi protocols (DEX swaps, lending, collateral liquidations)? Suggest practical risk mitigations.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ4
constructive_questions.Details: A user signs the wrong transaction or approves a malicious smart contract. Why is it hard to reverse on-chain?
